title: When do you choose interface vs abstract class: and why does Java 8+ blurring (default methods) still not make them interchangeable?
shortTitle: When do you choose interface vs abstract class?
keyPoints: Choose interface when defining a capability contract that unrelated classes can implement (Auditable, Comparable)
Choose abstract class when sharing mutable state (fields) and constructors among a family of related classes
Java 8 default methods narrowed the gap but interfaces still cannot have constructors or instance fields
Interface default methods are implicitly public: no protected access for family-only methods
A class can extend only one abstract class but implement unlimited interfaces
Modern guideline: default to interface; use abstract class only when you need constructors or shared mutable state

s1_definition.oneliner: Interface for capability contracts (multiple inheritance, no state). Abstract class for family hierarchies (shared state, constructors). Java 8 default methods help but still no constructors, no instance fields, no protected methods.
s1_definition.profdef:
The choice between interface and abstract class depends on four remaining differences after Java 8.

- **Choose interface** when: defining a capability contract that unrelated classes can implement (Auditable, Comparable, Serializable), you need multiple inheritance of type, or the contract has no mutable state.
- **Choose abstract class** when: sharing mutable state (fields) and constructors among a family of related classes (`SavingsAccount` and `CurrentAccount` share `balance`, `accountId`), or you need non-public methods (`protected` helper methods).
- **Why not interchangeable**: (1) interfaces cannot have constructors, (2) interfaces cannot have instance fields, (3) interface methods are implicitly `public` (no protected), (4) a class can extend only one abstract class.
- **Modern guideline**: default to interface. Use abstract class only when you need constructors or shared mutable instance fields.
s1_definition.analogy: Interface is like a banking license at National Bank of India: any institution (bank, fintech, cooperative) can hold it. Multiple licenses allowed. Abstract class is like a bank template with pre-filled forms and a vault (state): only branches of this bank can use it. You can only belong to one bank (single inheritance) but hold many licenses (multiple interfaces). Java 8 gave licenses the ability to include instructions (default methods), but licenses still cannot have a vault (state) or a reception desk (constructor).

sections.s6_takeaway:
Choose interface when defining a capability that unrelated classes can implement (Auditable, Comparable, Serializable) and you need multiple inheritance of type. Choose abstract class when sharing mutable state (balance field, auditLog list) and constructors among a family of related classes (SavingsAccount IS-A Account). Java 8 default methods narrowed the gap by adding method bodies to interfaces, but they are still not interchangeable.

The four remaining differences: interfaces cannot have instance fields (only public static final constants), cannot have constructors (no state initialization), default methods are implicitly public (no protected access for family-only methods), and a class can extend only one abstract class but implement unlimited interfaces.

Remember one sentence: default to interface for contracts and capabilities, and use abstract class only when you genuinely need constructors or shared mutable instance fields.
